questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (patient identification)
questions.q: Which pair of identifiers is appropriate for confirming a patient's identity before venipuncture?
options: Room number and bed number
Diagnosis and ordering provider
Full name and date of birth
Last name and room number
questions.explain: Two patient specific identifiers, such as full name and date of birth or a medical record number, must match the requisition and, for inpatients, the ID band. A room or bed number is never an identifier because patients move and rooms are reassigned.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (patient identification)
questions.q: How should an outpatient be asked to confirm identity?
options: Ask the patient to state their full name and date of birth
Ask 'Are you Maria Lopez?' and wait for a yes
Read the name aloud from the requisition
Check the name on the patient's insurance card only
questions.explain: Open ended questions require the patient to supply the information, which avoids a confused, hard of hearing or distracted patient simply agreeing. A yes or no question, or reading the name aloud, invites a false confirmation.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (patient identification)
questions.q: An inpatient has no identification band on the wrist. What should the phlebotomist do?
options: Collect the sample and label it from the door sign
Ask a visitor to confirm the patient's name
Tape a temporary label to the bed rail and draw
Ask the nurse to place an ID band before collecting
questions.explain: Inpatients must have an ID band matched to the requisition before collection. The phlebotomist notifies the nurse, who confirms identity and applies a band per facility policy. Door signs and visitors are not reliable identifiers.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (infection control, hand hygiene)
questions.q: When may an alcohol based hand rub be used instead of soap and water?
options: Only after caring for a C. difficile patient
When hands are not visibly soiled
When hands are visibly dirty with blood
Never, soap and water is always required
questions.explain: Alcohol based hand rub is the preferred method for routine hand hygiene when hands are not visibly soiled. Visible soiling requires soap and water, and so does caring for patients with C. difficile, because alcohol does not kill its spores.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (infection control, hand hygiene)
questions.q: A phlebotomist leaves the room of a patient with Clostridioides difficile. Which hand hygiene method is preferred?
options: Alcohol based hand rub only
Washing with soap and running water
Wiping hands with an alcohol prep pad
Putting on a new pair of gloves
questions.explain: C. difficile forms spores that alcohol does not reliably kill. Washing with soap and water physically removes them. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene, and an alcohol pad is not a hand hygiene method.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (infection control, gloves)
questions.q: When must gloves be changed during patient care?
options: Only at the end of each work shift
Only when they visibly tear or leak
After every third patient on the list
Between patients, with hand hygiene
questions.explain: Gloves are single use: they are changed between patients, and hand hygiene is performed after removal because gloves can have small defects and hands can be contaminated during removal. Wearing the same gloves for several patients spreads infection.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (sharps safety)
questions.q: When should the safety feature on a venipuncture needle be activated?
options: Right after the needle leaves the vein
After the tubes have been labeled
Before the needle first enters the skin
When the patient has left the room
questions.explain: The safety device is activated right after the needle leaves the vein, ideally with one hand, so the contaminated point is never exposed. Waiting until labeling or later leaves an exposed needle on the tray and raises the risk of a stick.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (sharps safety)
questions.q: What is the correct practice for a used venipuncture needle?
options: Recap it with both hands before discarding
Bend the needle so it cannot be reused
Do not recap; activate the safety device and discard it
Remove the needle from the holder by hand
questions.explain: OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard prohibits recapping, bending or removing contaminated needles unless no alternative exists. The safety device is engaged and the needle and holder go into a sharps container as one unit when designed for single use.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (sharps safety)
questions.q: When should a sharps container be replaced?
options: Only when it is completely full to the top
At the end of every shift regardless of level
When a needle sticks out of the opening
When it reaches the fill line marked on the container
questions.explain: Sharps containers are closed and replaced when contents reach the manufacturer's fill line, usually about three quarters full. Overfilling leads to needles protruding and sticks during disposal; a protruding needle means the container was already overfilled.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (needlestick exposure)
questions.q: A phlebotomist sustains a needlestick from a used needle. What is the first action?
options: Squeeze the wound and apply bleach
Wash the site with soap and water
Finish the draw and report at shift end
Cover the wound and continue working
questions.explain: First aid for a needlestick is to wash the area with soap and water right away, then report the exposure immediately so post exposure evaluation and any needed treatment can start promptly. Bleach and squeezing are not recommended, and delaying the report wastes valuable time.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (needlestick exposure)
questions.q: After first aid for a needlestick, why must the exposure be reported to the supervisor immediately?
options: So the patient can be billed for the event
So the phlebotomist can be scheduled off
So post exposure evaluation can begin quickly
So the needle brand can be changed
questions.explain: Under OSHA, employers must provide a confidential medical evaluation and follow up after an exposure incident. Some treatments, such as HIV post exposure prophylaxis, work best when started within hours, so prompt reporting matters.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard)
questions.q: Under OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard, what must the employer offer workers with occupational exposure?
options: Hepatitis B vaccination at no cost
Hepatitis C vaccination at no cost
HIV vaccination at reduced cost
Annual flu shots paid by the worker
questions.explain: Employers must offer the hepatitis B vaccine series free of charge to employees with occupational exposure, within 10 working days of initial assignment. There is no vaccine for hepatitis C or HIV. A worker may decline by signing a declination form.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard)
questions.q: How often must an employer's Exposure Control Plan be reviewed and updated under OSHA?
options: At least once a year
Every 5 years
Only after an exposure
Every 3 months
questions.explain: OSHA requires the Exposure Control Plan to be reviewed and updated at least annually and whenever tasks or procedures change. The review must consider safer medical devices and include input from frontline employees.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act)
questions.q: Which requirement was added by the Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act?
options: Free HIV vaccine for all healthcare workers
Recapping all needles using two hands
Safety engineered sharps and an injury log
Reusing needle holders after cleaning
questions.explain: The Act updated OSHA's standard to require evaluation and use of safety engineered sharps, a sharps injury log and input from frontline workers in choosing devices. Recapping with two hands is prohibited, and no HIV vaccine exists.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (standard precautions)
questions.q: What do standard precautions require?
options: Wearing gloves only for patients known to be infected
Treating all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious
Using precautions only in isolation rooms
Testing every patient for HIV before a draw
questions.explain: Standard precautions apply to every patient regardless of diagnosis, because infection status is often unknown. They include hand hygiene, gloves for contact with blood, and other PPE when splashes are likely.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (transmission based precautions)
questions.q: A patient is on contact precautions. Which PPE does the phlebotomist put on before entering?
options: N95 respirator only
Surgical mask only
Shoe covers only
Gown and gloves
questions.explain: Contact precautions, used for organisms such as MRSA, require a gown and gloves on entry. An N95 respirator is for airborne precautions, and a surgical mask is for droplet precautions.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (transmission based precautions)
questions.q: Which PPE is required for droplet precautions, used for illnesses such as influenza?
options: A fit tested N95 respirator
A gown only
A surgical mask
No PPE beyond gloves
questions.explain: Droplet precautions call for a surgical mask when entering the room, because large respiratory droplets travel only a short distance. An N95 respirator is required for airborne diseases such as tuberculosis, measles and chickenpox.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (transmission based precautions)
questions.q: A patient with suspected tuberculosis needs a blood draw. Which respiratory protection is required?
options: A fit tested N95 respirator
A standard surgical mask
A face shield alone
No mask if the patient wears one
questions.explain: Tuberculosis spreads by airborne particles, so airborne precautions apply: a fit tested N95 or higher respirator, and the patient is placed in an airborne infection isolation room. A surgical mask does not filter the smallest particles.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (PPE removal)
questions.q: According to CDC guidance, which item of PPE is usually removed first?
options: Mask
Goggles
Gown
Gloves
questions.explain: CDC's sequence removes the most contaminated item, gloves, first, then goggles or face shield, then gown, then mask or respirator, with hand hygiene at the end. An alternative method removes gown and gloves together. Removing the mask first risks touching the face with contaminated gloves.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (PPE donning)
questions.q: In CDC's recommended sequence for putting on PPE, which item goes on last?
options: Gown
Gloves
Mask
Goggles
questions.explain: PPE is put on as gown, mask or respirator, goggles or face shield, then gloves last, so the gloves can be pulled over the gown cuffs. Putting gloves on first would mean handling the other items with gloved hands and leaving gaps at the wrists.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (spill cleanup)
questions.q: Blood spills on the drawing station counter. Which disinfectant is appropriate after absorbing the spill?
options: Plain tap water followed by a dry paper towel
1:10 bleach or EPA registered disinfectant
70% alcohol sprayed on and wiped off at once
Hand lotion to loosen and lift the dried blood
questions.explain: After absorbing visible blood with gloves on, the area is disinfected with a freshly prepared 1:10 dilution of household bleach or an EPA registered disinfectant, left on for the labeled contact time. Water alone does not disinfect, and wiping alcohol off immediately does not allow contact time.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (biohazard waste)
questions.q: Which container is appropriate for blood soaked gauze?
options: A regular trash can with a lid
The nearest sharps disposal container
A paper recycling bin
A red or biohazard labeled waste bag
questions.explain: Gauze saturated with blood is regulated medical waste and goes in a red bag or biohazard labeled container. The sharps container is for needles and other sharps; filling it with soft waste wastes capacity and may violate policy.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (chain of infection)
questions.q: Performing hand hygiene between patients breaks which link of the chain of infection?
options: Mode of transmission
Infectious agent
Reservoir of the organism
Susceptible host
questions.explain: The chain of infection includes the infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry and susceptible host. Hand hygiene interrupts the mode of transmission because hands are a major way organisms travel between patients. Vaccination protects the susceptible host.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (bloodborne pathogens)
questions.q: Which bloodborne pathogen carries the highest risk of infection after a needlestick from an infected source when the worker is not immune?
options: HIV
Hepatitis C virus
Hepatitis B virus
Influenza virus
questions.explain: The risk of hepatitis B transmission after a needlestick from an infected source is far higher than for hepatitis C or HIV in an unvaccinated worker, and the virus can survive in dried blood for days. Vaccination greatly reduces this risk. Influenza is not a bloodborne pathogen.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (HIPAA)
questions.q: Which action complies with HIPAA privacy rules?
options: Talking about a patient's results in the elevator
Leaving requisitions face up at the waiting area
Posting a patient's name with a test on social media
Discussing results only with authorized staff who need them
questions.explain: HIPAA limits use and disclosure of protected health information to those who need it for treatment, payment or operations. Conversations in public areas, uncovered paperwork and social media posts can expose PHI.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (HIPAA)
questions.q: The HIPAA minimum necessary standard means what for a phlebotomist?
options: Draw the minimum blood volume for any test
Access only the information needed to do the job
Collect the fewest tubes possible per patient
Share results only with the patient's employer
questions.explain: The minimum necessary standard limits access to and disclosure of protected health information to what is needed for the task. It does not concern blood volumes. Employers are generally not entitled to results without patient authorization.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (quality control, supplies)
questions.q: Why must evacuated tube expiration dates be checked before use?
options: Expired tubes change color and confuse the order of draw
Expired tubes are heavier and harder to fill
Expired tubes may lose vacuum or have degraded additives
Expired tubes are fine if still sealed
questions.explain: After expiration, tubes may lose vacuum, causing short draws, and additives may break down, affecting results. Expired tubes are discarded. Sealing does not prevent the slow loss of vacuum over time.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (quality control, equipment)
questions.q: Why are daily temperature logs kept for a specimen refrigerator?
options: To document that specimens are stored in range
To track how often staff open the door
To record the number of specimens stored
To show when the refrigerator was cleaned
questions.explain: Temperature logs are a quality control record that shows specimens and reagents were kept within the required range. If a reading falls out of range, corrective action is taken and documented. Other records track cleaning or specimen counts.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (incident reporting)
questions.q: A phlebotomist realizes a tube was labeled with the wrong patient's name after it was sent. What is the appropriate action?
options: Report it to the supervisor and lab at once
Ignore it since the lab will catch it
Relabel the tube once it is back in the lab
Wait to see whether results look abnormal
questions.explain: Mislabeling can lead to wrong diagnoses or transfusion errors, so it must be reported at once so the specimen can be rejected and recollected. Incident reports support quality improvement. Relabeling a specimen after it leaves the patient is not acceptable.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (workplace safety)
questions.q: Which practice is required in areas where specimens are handled?
options: Food may be stored with specimens if wrapped
Drinks are allowed on the counter with lids
No eating, drinking or applying cosmetics
Snacks are allowed if gloves are worn
questions.explain: OSHA prohibits eating, drinking, smoking, applying cosmetics or lip balm and handling contact lenses where occupational exposure is likely. Food and drinks may not be stored in refrigerators or on counters where blood is present.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (fire safety)
questions.q: In the RACE fire response, what does the first letter stand for?
options: Run
Rescue
Report
Remove
questions.explain: RACE stands for Rescue, Alarm, Contain and Extinguish or Evacuate. The first step is to rescue anyone in immediate danger, then activate the alarm. Running or reporting are not the terms used in this sequence.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (fire safety)
questions.q: In the PASS method for a fire extinguisher, what does the A stand for?
options: Activate the alarm
Alert the supervisor
Approach from downwind
Aim at the base of the fire
questions.explain: PASS means Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle and Sweep side to side. Activating the alarm belongs to the RACE sequence, a separate memory aid used for the overall fire response.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (chemical safety)
questions.q: Where can a phlebotomist find hazard and first aid information for a chemical used in the lab?
options: The patient's requisition form
The centrifuge maintenance log
The Safety Data Sheet for that chemical
The tube manufacturer's color chart
questions.explain: Under OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard, employers keep Safety Data Sheets for hazardous chemicals, listing hazards, handling, PPE and first aid. The other documents do not provide chemical hazard information.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (exposure response)
questions.q: Blood splashes into a phlebotomist's eyes. How long should the eyes be flushed at the eyewash station?
options: At least 15 minutes
About 30 seconds
About 2 minutes
Until the stinging stops
questions.explain: Eyewash standards call for flushing for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelids open, followed by reporting the exposure. A short rinse may not remove all the material, and stinging can stop before the eye is clean.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (gloves)
questions.q: A glove tears during a venipuncture. Once the draw is safely completed, what should the phlebotomist do?
options: Cover the tear with tape and continue
Put a second glove over the torn one
Finish the shift with the torn glove
Change gloves after hand hygiene
questions.explain: A torn glove no longer protects the wearer. After the patient is safe, the gloves are removed, hand hygiene is performed and new gloves are put on. Taping or layering over a tear does not remove contamination that may already be on the skin.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (infection control, equipment)
questions.q: Why do many facilities use single use tourniquets?
options: Single use tourniquets apply more pressure
Reusable tourniquets can carry bacteria such as MRSA
Single use tourniquets are required for children only
Reusable tourniquets cause hemolysis
questions.explain: Studies have found reusable tourniquets contaminated with bacteria, including MRSA, so single use tourniquets help prevent transmission between patients. They do not change pressure or cause hemolysis.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (isolation procedures)
questions.q: Which practice is correct when collecting blood from a patient in contact isolation?
options: Bring the full tray into the room
Bring in only needed supplies
Skip hand hygiene since PPE is worn
Carry the specimens out without a bag
questions.explain: To prevent contamination, only the supplies needed are taken into the room, and the phlebotomy tray stays outside. Hand hygiene is still needed before and after PPE. Specimens are placed in a biohazard bag per facility policy.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (consent)
questions.q: After the phlebotomist explains the procedure, a patient silently rolls up a sleeve and extends an arm. What type of consent is this?
options: Informed written consent
Expressed verbal consent
Emergency consent
Implied consent
questions.explain: Implied consent is shown through actions, such as offering an arm after the procedure is explained, and is generally accepted for routine venipuncture. Informed written consent is used for more invasive procedures. The patient may still withdraw consent at any time.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (patient rights)
questions.q: A patient refuses to have blood drawn. What is the appropriate action?
options: Respect the refusal, notify the nurse or provider and document
Restrain the patient so the test can be done
Draw the blood while the patient is distracted
Tell the patient they have no right to refuse
questions.explain: Competent patients have the right to refuse procedures. The phlebotomist may explain the purpose but must not pressure or force the patient, and the refusal is reported to the nurse or provider and documented per policy.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Safety and Compliance (quality assurance)
questions.q: Which activity is an example of quality assurance in phlebotomy?
options: Choosing the fastest tube brand available
Drawing extra tubes in case of errors
Monitoring specimen rejection rates and correcting causes
Skipping documentation when the lab is busy
questions.explain: Quality assurance tracks indicators such as rejected specimens, recollections and patient identification errors, then addresses their causes. Drawing extra tubes without orders wastes blood, and skipping documentation undermines quality.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (requisitions)
questions.q: Which item must appear on a laboratory requisition?
options: The patient's employer
The phlebotomist's home phone
The patient's height and weight
The name of the ordering provider
questions.explain: A requisition identifies the patient, the ordering provider, the tests requested and other details such as date, special instructions and diagnosis codes for billing. Employer details and the collector's personal information are not required.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (fasting)
questions.q: A patient fasting for a lipid panel asks what may be consumed. Which is generally allowed during the fast?
options: Black coffee with sugar
Plain water
Chewing gum
A small glass of juice
questions.explain: During a typical 8 to 12 hour fast, plain water is usually allowed and helps keep veins full. Coffee with sugar, juice and gum can change glucose and other results, so they are avoided unless the provider instructs otherwise.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (fasting)
questions.q: A patient scheduled for a fasting glucose says he ate breakfast an hour ago. What should the phlebotomist do?
options: Collect it and label it fasting anyway
Send the patient home without telling anyone
Follow policy, such as contacting the provider, and document
Have the patient drink water and wait 15 minutes
questions.explain: A nonfasting sample can give misleading results. The phlebotomist follows facility policy, which often means notifying the provider for instructions and, if collected, clearly documenting that the patient was not fasting. Labeling it fasting would be falsification.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (patient positioning)
questions.q: Which position is appropriate for an outpatient venipuncture?
options: Seated in a drawing chair with an armrest
Standing at the counter with arm extended
Sitting on a stool with no arm support
Perched on the edge of an exam table
questions.explain: Patients should sit in a phlebotomy chair with an armrest that supports the arm and can prevent a fall if the patient faints, or lie down. Standing, sitting on a stool or perching on a table edge creates a fall risk.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (patient positioning)
questions.q: A patient says she has fainted during past blood draws. What is the best preparation?
options: Have her lie down for the procedure
Ask her to stand so it goes faster
Have her hold her breath during the draw
Use the arm on the side she sleeps on
questions.explain: Patients with a history of fainting should lie down, which keeps blood flowing to the brain and prevents falls. Standing increases the risk of injury, and holding the breath can contribute to lightheadedness.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (fainting)
questions.q: During a venipuncture, the seated patient becomes pale and says she feels faint. What should the phlebotomist do first?
options: Continue until all tubes are filled
Give her an ammonia inhalant right away
Release the tourniquet and remove the needle
Ask her to stand up and walk around
questions.explain: At the first sign of fainting, the procedure is stopped: tourniquet released, needle removed, pressure applied and the patient's head lowered or the patient lowered to lie down, with help called as needed. Continuing the draw or standing her up risks injury.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (vein selection)
questions.q: Which antecubital vein is usually the first choice for venipuncture?
options: Basilic
Median cubital
Cephalic
Accessory cephalic
questions.explain: The median cubital vein is generally large, well anchored and away from major nerves and arteries, so it is usually the first choice. The cephalic is second, and the basilic is last because it lies near the brachial artery and the median nerve. There is no radial vein used routinely.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (vein selection)
questions.q: Why is the basilic vein usually the last choice in the antecubital area?
options: It is the largest vein and bleeds too much
It is always too deep to reach with a needle
It cannot be used for evacuated tubes
It lies near the brachial artery and median nerve
questions.explain: The basilic vein runs close to the brachial artery and the median nerve and tends to roll, so arterial puncture and nerve injury are more likely. It can be used when no other vein is suitable, with extra care.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (contraindicated sites)
questions.q: A patient had a left mastectomy with lymph node removal. Which arm should be used?
options: The left arm
Either arm with a tighter tourniquet
The right arm
The left arm below the elbow
questions.explain: After a mastectomy with lymph node removal, the arm on that side is at risk of lymphedema and infection, and results can be affected. Blood is drawn from the opposite arm unless the provider gives permission otherwise.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (contraindicated sites)
questions.q: A patient has an IV infusing in the left forearm, and the right arm is available. Where should blood be drawn?
options: From the right arm
From the left arm above the IV
From the IV line itself
From the left arm right next to the IV
questions.explain: Drawing from the arm without an IV avoids contamination of the sample with IV fluid. If both arms have IVs, a draw below the IV after the infusion is stopped for a time set by policy may be done. Drawing above an IV is not acceptable.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (contraindicated sites)
questions.q: A dialysis patient has an arteriovenous fistula in the left arm. What is the rule for that arm?
options: Use it since the vein is large and easy
Draw from the fistula with a large needle
Use it only for blood cultures
Do not use it for venipuncture or a tourniquet
questions.explain: An AV fistula or graft is the patient's dialysis lifeline. Venipuncture or a tourniquet on that arm can damage it or cause clotting or infection. Blood is drawn from the other arm unless a physician directs otherwise.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (site selection)
questions.q: Why should an edematous (swollen) area be avoided for venipuncture?
options: Edema makes the blood clot faster
Tissue fluid can dilute and alter the sample
The skin is too thin to cleanse properly
Edema raises the patient's blood pressure
questions.explain: Edematous tissue contains excess fluid that can contaminate the specimen and change results. Veins are also hard to find and the site may heal poorly. Another site is chosen.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (site selection)
questions.q: A patient has a large bruise from a previous draw in the right antecubital area. What should the phlebotomist do?
options: Draw directly through the bruise
Choose another site away from the hematoma
Apply the tourniquet over the bruise
Massage the bruise to find the vein
questions.explain: Drawing through a hematoma is painful and can yield old blood or hemolyzed samples. Another site is chosen; if that area must be used, the draw is made below the hematoma. Massaging the bruise does not help.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (site selection)
questions.q: Which area should be avoided when selecting a venipuncture site?
options: The median cubital vein of the non dominant arm
Veins on the back of the hand
The cephalic vein on the thumb side
Areas with extensive scars or burns
questions.explain: Scarred or burned tissue is hard to penetrate, veins are difficult to feel and healing and infection risks are greater. Hand veins and the cephalic vein are acceptable alternatives when antecubital veins are not suitable.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (latex allergy)
questions.q: A patient states a latex allergy. Which step is correct?
options: Use latex free gloves, tourniquet and bandage
Use latex gloves but a latex free bandage
Place gauze between skin and a latex tourniquet
Proceed normally since contact is brief
questions.explain: For a patient with latex allergy, all items that touch the patient, including gloves, tourniquet and bandage, must be latex free, and the room should be free of latex products. Even brief contact can trigger a severe reaction.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (vein palpation)
questions.q: How does a suitable vein usually feel when palpated?
options: Pulsating with each heartbeat
Hard and cordlike
Bouncy and resilient
Rigid like a tendon
questions.explain: A good vein feels bouncy or springy. A pulse means an artery, which must not be used for routine venipuncture. A hard, cordlike vein may be sclerosed or thrombosed, and tendons feel rigid.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (tourniquet application)
questions.q: Where is a tourniquet placed for an antecubital venipuncture?
options: Directly over the intended site
At the wrist below the site
About 10 inches above the elbow
About 3 to 4 inches above the intended site
questions.explain: The tourniquet goes about 3 to 4 inches above the puncture site, tight enough to slow venous return but not arterial flow. Too close to the site can make veins collapse when the needle goes in, and too far up has little effect.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (vein selection aids)
questions.q: Which technique can help make a patient's veins more prominent?
options: Raising the arm above the heart
Lowering the arm and applying a warm compress
Having the patient pump the fist hard
Applying ice to the antecubital area
questions.explain: Gravity and warmth increase blood flow to the veins. Raising the arm or applying ice does the opposite. Vigorous fist pumping is avoided because it can falsely raise potassium and other results.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (patient preparation)
questions.q: Why should a patient not repeatedly pump the fist before venipuncture?
options: It causes the needle to bend
It lowers the blood glucose
It can falsely raise potassium levels
It prevents the tourniquet from working
questions.explain: Repeated fist clenching causes muscle cells to release potassium, which can falsely elevate the result. The patient may make a gentle fist, but pumping is avoided. It does not affect the needle or glucose.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (vein selection)
questions.q: Antecubital veins are unusable, but good veins are visible on the back of the hand. Which equipment is usually preferred?
options: A winged set with a smaller gauge needle
A large gauge needle with a syringe
A capillary lancet for all tubes
A 16 gauge needle for faster flow
questions.explain: Hand veins are smaller and more fragile, so a winged (butterfly) set with a smaller needle, often 23 gauge, is commonly used. A 16 gauge needle is far too large, and capillary collection cannot provide multiple venous tubes.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (pediatric patients)
questions.q: During venipuncture on a young child, what is the role of a parent or second staff member?
options: Helping keep the child still and comforted
Holding the tubes while the needle is placed
Choosing which vein should be used
Applying the tourniquet for the phlebotomist
questions.explain: Children may move suddenly, risking injury. A second person helps immobilize and comfort the child, following facility policy. Equipment handling and vein selection remain the phlebotomist's responsibility.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (alternate sites)
questions.q: Antecubital and hand veins are unavailable. What is usually required before drawing from a vein in the foot or leg?
options: Approval from the patient's family
A second phlebotomist to confirm the vein
Permission from the provider per facility policy
Nothing, since leg veins are first choice
questions.explain: Leg, ankle and foot veins carry a higher risk of clots and infection, especially in patients with diabetes or poor circulation, so most facilities require a provider's permission before using them. They are never first choice.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (patient preparation)
questions.q: An inpatient is asleep when the phlebotomist arrives. What should be done?
options: Draw the blood without waking the patient
Wake the patient gently and confirm identity
Ask the roommate to confirm the name
Use the name on the door sign
questions.explain: A sleeping patient might startle and move, risking injury, and cannot confirm identity or consent. The patient is gently awakened and identified with two identifiers before the procedure. Roommates and door signs are not reliable.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (patient preparation)
questions.q: A patient taking an anticoagulant has blood drawn. What adjustment is usually needed after the needle is removed?
options: Apply no pressure to avoid bruising
Have the patient bend the elbow tightly
Wrap a tourniquet over the site
Apply pressure longer until bleeding stops
questions.explain: Anticoagulants prolong bleeding, so pressure is held longer and the site checked to make sure bleeding has stopped before bandaging. Bending the elbow can reopen the puncture and cause a hematoma.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (preanalytical variables)
questions.q: What does the term basal state mean for blood collection?
options: Immediately after exercise and a meal
Late afternoon after a normal lunch
Early morning, rested, after fasting about 12 hours
Any time after taking all medications
questions.explain: The basal state is the body's resting metabolic condition early in the morning after about 12 hours of fasting. Many reference ranges are based on it. Exercise, meals and time of day change many analytes.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (preanalytical variables)
questions.q: Strenuous exercise before a blood draw can raise which test result?
options: Creatine kinase (CK)
Hemoglobin A1c
Blood type
Hepatitis B antibody
questions.explain: Muscle exertion releases enzymes such as creatine kinase into the blood, so strenuous exercise can raise CK for a day or more. Hemoglobin A1c reflects average glucose over months, and blood type and antibodies are not affected by exercise.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (elderly patients)
questions.q: An elderly patient has thin skin and fragile veins. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Use a large needle and a very tight tourniquet
Slap the vein repeatedly to raise it
Pull the skin firmly upward to anchor
Use a smaller needle and a loosely applied tourniquet
questions.explain: Fragile veins can collapse or blow, and thin skin bruises and tears easily. A smaller needle or winged set, a gently applied tourniquet (sometimes over a sleeve) and careful anchoring reduce injury. Slapping can cause bruising and hemolysis.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (preparation for timed tests)
questions.q: Why is cortisol often ordered at a specific time of day?
options: It is unstable after noon
Its level varies in a daily rhythm
It requires an empty stomach
It can only be measured in the evening
questions.explain: Cortisol shows diurnal variation, typically highest in the morning and lower later in the day, so the collection time must match the order for correct interpretation. Timing, not stability or fasting, is the main concern.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (anxious patients)
questions.q: A patient says she is very nervous about needles. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Tell her not to look and start without warning
Explain each step calmly and offer to let her lie down
Ask a stranger in the waiting room to hold her arm
Reschedule the draw without telling the provider
questions.explain: Calm explanation builds trust and lets the patient know what to expect, and lying down reduces the risk of injury if anxiety leads to fainting. Starting without warning can cause sudden movement and injury, and strangers should not be involved.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (fainting risk)
questions.q: Which question asked before the draw helps identify a patient's risk of fainting?
options: Which arm do you write with most days?
Did you bring your insurance card today?
Do you prefer a morning or afternoon visit?
Have you ever felt faint during a blood draw?
questions.explain: A history of fainting or feeling faint during previous draws is a strong predictor of another episode. Knowing it in advance lets the phlebotomist position the patient lying down. Handedness can guide site choice, but it does not predict fainting.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Patient Preparation (equipment preparation)
questions.q: Before entering the patient's room, how does the phlebotomist decide which tubes to bring?
options: By matching tubes to the tests on the requisition
By bringing one of every tube color available
By asking the patient which tubes they prefer
By using the same tubes as the previous patient
questions.explain: The requisition lists the tests ordered, and each test requires a particular tube type and volume, per the laboratory's test directory. Bringing tubes at random wastes supplies and invites errors, and patients cannot select tube types.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (order of draw, CLSI GP41)
questions.q: According to the CLSI order of draw for venipuncture, which specimen is collected first?
options: Light blue sodium citrate tube
Lavender EDTA tube
Blood culture bottles
Gold serum separator tube
questions.explain: Blood cultures are collected first to keep them sterile and free of additive carryover. The sequence then continues with sodium citrate, serum tubes, heparin, EDTA and glycolytic inhibitor tubes.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (order of draw, CLSI GP41)
questions.q: Orders call for a PT/INR and a comprehensive metabolic panel in a gold SST. Which tube is drawn first?
options: The gold serum separator tube
Either tube, the order does not matter
A lavender tube before both
The light blue sodium citrate tube
questions.explain: In the CLSI order of draw, sodium citrate (light blue) comes before serum tubes, because clot activator carried into the citrate tube can affect coagulation results. No lavender tube was ordered, and the order of draw does matter.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (order of draw, CLSI GP41)
questions.q: A green heparin tube and a lavender EDTA tube are ordered. In what sequence are they drawn?
options: Lavender, then green
Green, then lavender
Either order is acceptable
Lavender, with green from a separate stick
questions.explain: Heparin tubes are drawn before EDTA tubes. EDTA carried into the heparin tube would bind calcium and add potassium, producing falsely low calcium and falsely high potassium in the chemistry results.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (order of draw, CLSI GP41)
questions.q: Where does the gray sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate tube fall in the CLSI order of draw?
options: First, before blood cultures
Right after the light blue tube
Last, after the EDTA tube
Between the serum and heparin tubes
questions.explain: Glycolytic inhibitor tubes such as gray tops are drawn last. Their additives, including oxalate and fluoride, could otherwise contaminate other tubes and interfere with tests such as electrolytes and enzyme assays.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (order of draw, CLSI GP41)
questions.q: Which sequence follows the CLSI order of draw?
options: Culture, light blue, gold, green, lavender, gray
Culture, gold, light blue, lavender, green, gray
Light blue, culture, green, gold, gray, lavender
Lavender, light blue, culture, gold, green, gray
questions.explain: The CLSI order is blood cultures, sodium citrate (light blue), serum tubes with or without clot activator or gel (red, gold), heparin (green), EDTA (lavender) and glycolytic inhibitor (gray). Placing gold before light blue risks clot activator reaching the coagulation tube.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (order of draw, additive carryover)
questions.q: If EDTA carries over into a chemistry tube, which result pattern is most likely?
options: Falsely high potassium and falsely low calcium
Falsely low potassium and falsely high calcium
Falsely high glucose and sodium
No change, since EDTA is inert
questions.explain: The most common EDTA salt contains potassium and binds calcium. Carryover into a chemistry tube can therefore raise potassium and lower calcium falsely. Following the order of draw prevents this.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (tube additives)
questions.q: Which additive is in a light blue top tube used for coagulation testing?
options: Sodium heparin
K2 EDTA
Sodium citrate
Sodium fluoride
questions.explain: Light blue tubes contain buffered sodium citrate, which binds calcium reversibly so clotting factors can be measured in tests such as PT/INR and aPTT. Heparin and EDTA are not used for routine coagulation testing.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (tube filling)
questions.q: Why must a light blue sodium citrate tube be filled to its indicated volume?
options: To make sure the blood clots completely
To keep the 9:1 blood to additive ratio
To prevent the gel barrier from moving
To keep the tube from breaking in the centrifuge
questions.explain: Coagulation tests depend on a 9:1 ratio of blood to citrate. An underfilled tube has excess citrate, which falsely prolongs clotting times, so labs reject short draws. Light blue tubes do not contain gel and are meant to stay anticoagulated.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (winged collection sets)
questions.q: A winged set is used, and a light blue tube is the first tube needed. What should be done first?
options: Fill the light blue tube first with no discard
Tap the tubing to remove air before the stick
Use a syringe and push blood into the tube
Draw a discard tube to fill the tubing's air space
questions.explain: The tubing of a winged set holds air. If the light blue tube is drawn first, that air takes up vacuum and causes underfilling. A discard tube, plain or citrate, is drawn first to prime the tubing. Pushing blood with a syringe plunger can hemolyze cells.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (tube additives and tests)
questions.q: Which tube is typically used for a complete blood count (CBC)?
options: Light blue top with citrate
Gray top with fluoride
Lavender top with EDTA
Red top with clot activator
questions.explain: EDTA preserves the shape of blood cells and prevents clotting, so lavender tubes are standard for CBCs and hemoglobin A1c. Citrate is for coagulation, gray for glucose and red for serum tests.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (tube additives and tests)
questions.q: Why is a gray top tube with sodium fluoride often used for glucose testing?
options: Fluoride inhibits glycolysis by blood cells
Fluoride makes the blood clot faster
Fluoride removes lipids from the sample
Fluoride protects glucose from light
questions.explain: Blood cells keep using glucose after collection, so glucose falls in an unseparated sample. Sodium fluoride inhibits glycolysis and preserves glucose, while potassium oxalate acts as the anticoagulant.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (tube additives and tests)
questions.q: Which additive is in a green top tube?
options: Sodium citrate
EDTA
Clot activator
Heparin
questions.explain: Green tubes contain lithium or sodium heparin, which inhibits thrombin, and are used for plasma chemistry tests. Light green tubes also contain a gel separator. EDTA is in lavender tubes and citrate in light blue tubes.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (serum tubes)
questions.q: What does a gold serum separator tube (SST) contain?
options: EDTA and a gel separator
Clot activator and a gel separator
Lithium heparin and a gel separator
Buffered sodium citrate only
questions.explain: An SST contains a clot activator to speed clotting and a gel that forms a barrier between serum and cells during centrifugation. Because it yields serum, it is drawn with serum tubes, after citrate and before heparin.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (serum tubes)
questions.q: Where do plastic red top tubes with clot activator fall in the order of draw?
options: Before blood culture bottles
After light blue, before heparin
After the gray tube at the very end
Between EDTA and gray tubes
questions.explain: Red plastic tubes contain a clot activator and belong with the serum tubes, drawn after sodium citrate and before heparin, EDTA and gray tubes. Drawing them before the light blue tube could carry clot activator into the coagulation specimen.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (tourniquet time)
questions.q: What is the maximum time a tourniquet should remain in place during venipuncture?
options: 3 minutes
5 minutes
2 minutes
1 minute
questions.explain: A tourniquet should stay on no longer than 1 minute. Longer application causes hemoconcentration, which can change many results. If more time is needed to find a vein, it is released and reapplied after about 2 minutes.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (tourniquet effects)
questions.q: Leaving the tourniquet on too long can cause which effect?
options: Hemoconcentration of the sample
Hemodilution with falsely low proteins
Clotting of blood at the needle tip
Falsely lower potassium in the sample
questions.explain: Prolonged tourniquet time pushes fluid out of the vein, concentrating cells, proteins and protein bound substances, so results such as total protein and cholesterol can be falsely high. Potassium may also rise rather than fall.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (needle insertion)
questions.q: At what angle is the needle usually inserted for a routine venipuncture?
options: 45 to 60 degrees
90 degrees
30 degrees or less
Parallel to the skin at 0 degrees
questions.explain: A shallow angle, typically 15 to 30 degrees, places the needle into the vein without passing through it. A steeper angle risks going through the back wall of the vein and causing a hematoma.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (needle insertion)
questions.q: Which way should the needle bevel face during venipuncture?
options: Down
Toward the thumb
It does not matter
Up
questions.explain: With the bevel up, the sharp point enters the skin first and smoothly, causing less pain and making it easier to enter the vein. Bevel down can catch the vein wall and block blood flow.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (anchoring the vein)
questions.q: How is a vein properly anchored before needle insertion?
options: Index finger presses directly on the site
Thumb below the site pulls skin taut toward the hand
Thumb above the site pulls skin toward the shoulder
Two fingers form a V over the site
questions.explain: Placing the thumb about 1 to 2 inches below the site and pulling the skin taut toward the hand keeps the vein from rolling. A finger over the site gets in the needle's path, and the V method risks a needlestick if the patient moves.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (site cleansing)
questions.q: Why must the alcohol be allowed to air dry before the puncture?
options: To make the vein easier to see
To keep the tourniquet from slipping
To disinfect well and avoid hemolysis
To prevent the blood from clotting in the tube
questions.explain: Alcohol needs time to dry to disinfect effectively. Puncturing through wet alcohol stings and can hemolyze the sample. Blowing on or fanning the site would recontaminate it.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (needle removal)
questions.q: When is the tourniquet released relative to needle removal?
options: Before the needle is removed
After the needle is removed
After the bandage is applied
After the patient leaves
questions.explain: The tourniquet is released before the needle is withdrawn, usually as the last tube fills. Removing the needle with the tourniquet on forces blood out of the puncture and causes a hematoma.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (post puncture care)
questions.q: After the needle is withdrawn, how should pressure be applied?
options: With gauze while the arm stays straight
With the arm bent tightly at the elbow
With an alcohol pad on the site
No pressure, just a bandage at once
questions.explain: Firm pressure with clean gauze and the arm extended or slightly raised helps the puncture seal. Bending the elbow can reopen the site and cause bruising, and alcohol pads sting and slow clotting.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (tube mixing)
questions.q: How should additive tubes be mixed after collection?
options: Shaken vigorously for 10 seconds
Rolled slowly an hour later
Gently inverted right away
Left untouched until centrifuging
questions.explain: Additive tubes are gently inverted immediately so the additive mixes with the blood, the number following manufacturer instructions. Vigorous shaking causes hemolysis, and delayed mixing can allow clots to form in anticoagulated tubes.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (hemolysis)
questions.q: Which practice is a common cause of hemolyzed specimens?
options: Using the median cubital vein
Shaking the tubes vigorously
Drawing tubes in the correct order
Allowing the alcohol to dry first
questions.explain: Vigorous shaking ruptures red cells. Other causes include puncturing through wet alcohol, very small needles, forcing blood through a syringe needle and pulling hard on a syringe plunger. The other options are good practice.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (hemolysis effects)
questions.q: Hemolysis most notably raises which test result?
options: Sodium
Glucose
Albumin
Potassium
questions.explain: Red blood cells contain much more potassium than plasma. When they rupture, potassium is released and the result is falsely high, so labs often reject hemolyzed specimens for potassium.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (complications, hematoma)
questions.q: Which situation most often leads to a hematoma during venipuncture?
options: The tourniquet is applied 3 to 4 inches above the site
The patient is seated in a drawing chair
The needle passes through the back wall of the vein
The bevel faces up during insertion
questions.explain: Blood leaks into tissue when the needle goes through the vein, only partly enters it or when pressure afterward is inadequate. Removing the needle before releasing the tourniquet also causes hematomas. The other options are correct technique.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (complications, arterial puncture)
questions.q: During a draw, the blood is bright red and pulses into the tube. What is the appropriate action?
options: Remove the needle and apply firm pressure
Continue and label the tubes as venous
Apply a second tourniquet above the site
Raise the arm and leave the site uncovered
questions.explain: Bright red, pulsing blood suggests an arterial puncture. The needle is removed and firm pressure applied for at least about 5 minutes, until bleeding stops, and the event is reported. Arterial blood should not be labeled as venous.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (complications, nerve injury)
questions.q: A patient reports a sharp, electric pain shooting down the arm during the draw. What should the phlebotomist do?
options: Probe gently to find a better spot
Ask the patient to hold still a minute
Tighten the tourniquet and continue
Remove the needle immediately
questions.explain: Shooting or electric pain suggests nerve contact. The needle is removed immediately to avoid permanent injury, pressure is applied and the event is documented. Probing increases nerve damage.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (troubleshooting)
questions.q: Blood flow stops partway through filling a tube, and the needle seems correctly placed. What is a reasonable first step?
options: Probe in several directions to find the vein
Try a new tube in case the first lost its vacuum
Remove the needle and stick the other arm
Leave the tube on until it fills
questions.explain: A tube that has lost vacuum will stop filling. Trying a new tube is a simple first check. Blind probing is painful and risks nerve or artery injury, and a new puncture is not needed before simple checks.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (venipuncture attempts)
questions.q: Under common practice, after two unsuccessful attempts by one phlebotomist, what should happen?
options: Keep trying until blood is obtained
Another phlebotomist tries, per policy
Draw from a nearby artery instead
Collect the sample from the IV line
questions.explain: Common facility policies, based on CLSI guidance, limit a phlebotomist to two attempts. Another qualified person then tries, or the provider is notified. Repeated sticks cause pain and injury.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (syringe collection)
questions.q: What is the safe way to fill tubes from a syringe draw?
options: Push the needle through the stopper and press hard
Remove stoppers and squirt blood into the tubes
Pour blood from the syringe into the tubes
Use a syringe transfer device and let the vacuum fill tubes
questions.explain: A transfer device prevents needlesticks, and letting each tube's vacuum draw the blood keeps the correct volume. Forcing blood with the plunger can hemolyze cells and pop stoppers. Removing stoppers breaks the closed system.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (needle gauge)
questions.q: Which statement about needle gauge is correct?
options: A higher gauge number means a smaller diameter
A higher gauge number means a larger diameter
Gauge refers to the length of the needle
All venipuncture needles share one gauge
questions.explain: Gauge is inversely related to diameter: a 23 gauge needle is smaller than a 21 gauge. A 21 gauge is common for routine adult venipuncture. Length is measured separately in inches.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (capillary puncture sites)
questions.q: Which area is appropriate for a heel puncture on an infant?
options: The center of the back of the heel
The middle of the arch of the foot
Medial or lateral plantar heel surface
The fleshy tip of the big toe
questions.explain: Heel punctures are made on the medial or lateral plantar surface, where the heel bone is deeper. The back curve of the heel, the arch and toes are avoided because bone, nerves or tendons lie close to the skin.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (capillary puncture sites)
questions.q: For an adult fingerstick, which site is preferred?
options: The center of the thumb's fleshy pad
The tip of the index finger nail bed
The fifth finger close to the nail edge
Side of the middle or ring finger pad
questions.explain: The middle and ring fingers of the non dominant hand are preferred, puncturing slightly to the side of the fleshy pad, across the fingerprint lines so blood forms a drop. The thumb has a pulse, the fifth finger has little tissue and the index finger is often calloused.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (capillary puncture technique)
questions.q: Why is the first drop of blood usually wiped away in a capillary puncture?
options: It contains too few red blood cells
It may contain tissue fluid and alcohol
It is always hemolyzed by the lancet
It clots before reaching the container
questions.explain: The first drop can be contaminated with tissue fluid and residual alcohol, which affect results, so it is usually wiped away unless the test instructions say otherwise. Collection begins with the second drop.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (capillary order of draw)
questions.q: When several microcollection containers are filled from one skin puncture, which is generally collected first?
options: The serum container
The gray fluoride container
The EDTA container
The green heparin container
questions.explain: For skin puncture, CLSI recommends filling the EDTA container first, because platelets clump quickly at the site. Other additive containers come next and serum containers last. This differs from the venipuncture order.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (capillary puncture technique)
questions.q: Why should the finger or heel not be squeezed hard during capillary collection?
options: It causes hemolysis and tissue fluid dilution
It makes the puncture site close up faster
It increases the blood glucose falsely
It changes the color of the blood drops
questions.explain: Strong squeezing, or milking, breaks red cells and forces tissue fluid into the sample, which can change potassium and other results. Gentle, intermittent pressure is acceptable.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (capillary puncture technique)
questions.q: Why is a site warmed before a capillary puncture?
options: To increase blood flow to the area
To sterilize the skin surface
To make the skin thicker
To slow the flow of blood
questions.explain: Warming the site, for example with a commercial heel warmer for a few minutes, can increase blood flow several times over and makes collection easier. It does not sterilize the skin; cleansing with alcohol is still needed.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (heel puncture depth)
questions.q: What is the maximum recommended depth of a heel puncture on an infant?
options: 3.5 mm
5.0 mm
2.0 mm
1 cm
questions.explain: CLSI recommends heel punctures no deeper than 2.0 mm to avoid reaching the heel bone, which can cause osteomyelitis. Devices made for infants are designed to control depth.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (capillary puncture limits)
questions.q: Which test generally cannot be collected by capillary puncture?
options: Blood glucose
Blood cultures
Hemoglobin
Newborn screening
questions.explain: Blood cultures require larger volumes collected by venipuncture into culture bottles. Glucose, hemoglobin and newborn screening are routinely performed on capillary blood.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (specimen quality)
questions.q: A lavender tube for a CBC arrives with small clots. What is the most likely cause?
options: Drawing the tube before the gray tube
Using a standard 21 gauge needle
Labeling the tube at the bedside
Inadequate mixing after collection
questions.explain: EDTA must mix with blood right away. If the tube is not inverted promptly, small clots can form, making the CBC invalid. Drawing lavender before gray is the correct order, and needle size and bedside labeling are good practice.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Routine Blood Collections (venipuncture procedure)
questions.q: What is the first step before approaching a patient for venipuncture?
options: Apply the tourniquet
Select the needle size
Review the requisition
Cleanse the site
questions.explain: The phlebotomist begins by reviewing the requisition for the tests ordered, special requirements and patient information. Patient identification follows, then hand hygiene, gloves, vein selection and cleansing.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (blood cultures)
questions.q: Before collecting blood cultures, what is done to the culture bottle tops?
options: Remove the caps and disinfect the tops with alcohol
Leave the caps on and puncture through them
Wipe the tops with povidone iodine and leave it
Rinse the tops with sterile water
questions.explain: The protective caps are removed, and the septum is disinfected, usually with 70% alcohol, and allowed to dry. Iodine left on the stopper can damage some bottles. Contamination of the tops can cause false positive cultures.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (blood cultures)
questions.q: Blood cultures are collected with a winged set. Which bottle is usually filled first?
options: The anaerobic bottle
Either bottle, the order does not matter
A gold SST before either bottle
The aerobic bottle
questions.explain: With a winged set, air in the tubing enters the first bottle. Filling the aerobic bottle first keeps that air out of the anaerobic bottle, where oxygen would hinder anaerobic organisms. Cultures come before any other tubes.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (blood cultures)
questions.q: Why are blood culture sets commonly drawn from two separate sites?
options: To make sure the patient is not anemic
To help tell true infection from skin contamination
To double the volume for chemistry tests
To allow one bottle to be discarded
questions.explain: When the same organism grows in sets from separate venipunctures, it is more likely a true infection. Growth in only one set of a common skin organism suggests contamination. Culture volumes are not used for chemistry tests.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (blood cultures)
questions.q: Why must the skin antiseptic dry fully before a blood culture puncture?
options: Wet skin can crack the culture bottles
Drying is part of how it kills microbes
Dry skin raises the culture volume
It prevents the blood from clotting
questions.explain: Antiseptics such as chlorhexidine need contact time and drying to work. Puncturing too early increases the chance of skin bacteria entering the bottle and causing a false positive. The site is not touched again after cleansing.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (glucose tolerance test)
questions.q: How does an oral glucose tolerance test begin?
options: With the glucose drink, then a fasting draw
With a random draw after breakfast
With a urine sample only
With a fasting blood specimen
questions.explain: The OGTT starts with a fasting blood specimen; the glucose drink is given after that baseline, often after the fasting result is checked per protocol, and timed draws follow. A nonfasting start would invalidate the test.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (glucose tolerance test)
questions.q: During an oral glucose tolerance test, what instruction is given to the patient between draws?
options: Rest without food, smoking or gum
Go for a brisk walk outside the building
Eat a light snack if hungry
Drink coffee to stay awake
questions.explain: Food, smoking, gum, caffeinated drinks and exercise can change glucose levels, so the patient stays seated or at rest in the facility. Many protocols allow water. Leaving or exercising would distort results.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (glucose tolerance test)
questions.q: A patient vomits shortly after drinking the glucose solution for an OGTT. What should the phlebotomist do?
options: Give a second drink and keep the schedule
Continue the draws and say nothing
Notify the provider before continuing
Have the patient eat to settle the stomach
questions.explain: If the patient vomits, the amount of glucose absorbed is unknown, so results may not be valid. The provider or lab is notified to decide whether to stop or reschedule, and the event is documented.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (therapeutic drug monitoring)
questions.q: When is a trough level for therapeutic drug monitoring collected?
options: Immediately after the dose is finished
At any time of day
Two days after the last dose
Just before the next scheduled dose
questions.explain: A trough is the lowest drug concentration, so it is collected shortly before the next dose. A peak is collected after the dose is absorbed or infused, at a time that depends on the drug and route.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (therapeutic drug monitoring)
questions.q: Which information is essential to record with a therapeutic drug monitoring specimen?
options: The patient's favorite drink
Collection time and time of the last dose
The tube manufacturer's lot only
The phlebotomist's years of experience
questions.explain: Drug levels are interpreted in relation to dose timing. The exact collection time and the time the last dose was given allow the provider to judge whether the level is a true peak or trough.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (therapeutic drug monitoring)
questions.q: Why does peak level timing depend on the drug?
options: All drugs peak exactly one hour after a dose
Peak levels are always drawn at midnight
Absorption differs by drug and route
Only oral drugs have peak levels
questions.explain: The highest concentration occurs at different times depending on the drug, its form and route of administration. Collection times are set by the laboratory or prescriber for each drug. There is no single timing that fits all.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (chain of custody)
questions.q: What is the purpose of a chain of custody form for a forensic specimen?
options: To record each person who handled it
To list the tests the patient can afford
To record insurance information
To replace the requisition
questions.explain: A chain of custody form records every person who collects, transfers and receives the specimen, with dates and times, so results can stand up in legal proceedings. Any gap can make the result unusable.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (chain of custody)
questions.q: In a chain of custody urine drug collection, why is a tamper evident seal applied to the container?
options: To show it was not opened or altered
To keep the urine from freezing
To identify the price of the test
To protect the printed label from water
questions.explain: A tamper evident seal is placed over the cap, initialed by the donor and dated, so any opening would be visible. This protects the integrity of the specimen. Temperature and pricing are unrelated.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (chain of custody)
questions.q: In a federally regulated urine drug collection, within what time after voiding is the specimen temperature checked?
options: Within 30 minutes
Within 1 hour
Within 4 minutes
Before the donor voids
questions.explain: Federal drug testing procedures require reading the specimen temperature within 4 minutes of collection; an acceptable range is 32°C to 38°C. A reading outside the range may indicate a substituted specimen.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (newborn screening)
questions.q: How should blood be applied to a newborn screening filter paper card?
options: Several small drops layered in each circle
One large drop per circle from one side, soaking through
Blood applied to both sides of the paper
Blood smeared with a capillary tube
questions.explain: Each circle is filled with a single large drop applied to one side only, allowed to soak through to fill the circle completely. Layering drops, applying to both sides or touching the paper with devices causes uneven samples and rejection.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (newborn screening)
questions.q: How is a completed newborn screening card dried?
options: In a stack with the other cards from the unit
Under a heat lamp for faster drying
In a sealed plastic bag right away
Flat at room temperature, away from heat
questions.explain: Cards dry horizontally at room temperature, away from heat and direct sunlight, and are not stacked or sealed in plastic while wet. Heat damages analytes and moisture promotes degradation.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (newborn screening)
questions.q: Newborn screening specimens are generally collected at what age?
options: Within the first hour after birth
At the two week checkup only
24 to 48 hours after birth
At six months of age
questions.explain: Collection between 24 and 48 hours after birth allows enough feeding and metabolic activity for conditions such as phenylketonuria to show, while still allowing early treatment. Very early samples may give false negatives, and a repeat may be required.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (temperature sensitive specimens)
questions.q: How should a specimen for cold agglutinins be handled after collection?
options: Kept at 37°C until serum is separated
Placed in an ice and water slurry at once
Frozen at the bedside immediately
Left in a sunny window to stay warm
questions.explain: Cold agglutinins attach to red cells at cold temperatures. If the specimen cools before serum is separated, the antibodies bind to the cells and the result is falsely low. The tube is prewarmed and kept at 37°C.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (chilled specimens)
questions.q: A plasma ammonia is ordered. How is the specimen usually handled?
options: Kept at body temperature in a warmer
Left at room temperature for about 4 hours
Protected from light with foil only
Chilled in an ice slurry and sent at once
questions.explain: Ammonia levels rise in standing blood as cells metabolize, so the specimen is chilled in an ice and water slurry and delivered to the lab immediately for prompt processing. Warming is used for cold agglutinins, not ammonia.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (light sensitive specimens)
questions.q: Which specimen must be protected from light after collection?
options: Potassium
Bilirubin
Glucose
Hemoglobin
questions.explain: Bilirubin breaks down when exposed to light, leading to falsely low results, so the tube is wrapped in foil or an amber container is used. Vitamins such as B12 and A are also light sensitive.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Special Collections (blood alcohol collection)
questions.q: Which skin antiseptic should be avoided when collecting a blood alcohol specimen?
options: Soap and water
Isopropyl alcohol
Povidone iodine
Chlorhexidine without alcohol
questions.explain: Alcohol based antiseptics could contaminate the specimen and raise the result, which matters especially in legal cases. A nonalcohol antiseptic is used, and the tube is filled and kept tightly stoppered so alcohol does not evaporate.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Processing (clotting time)
questions.q: How long should a serum tube generally stand upright at room temperature before centrifugation?
options: About 2 minutes
About 4 hours
Overnight in a rack
About 30 minutes
questions.explain: Serum tubes need time to clot completely, generally about 30 minutes at room temperature for tubes with clot activator, longer for patients on anticoagulants. Spinning too early leaves fibrin strands, and long delays can alter results.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Processing (separation time)
questions.q: Within what time after collection should serum or plasma generally be separated from cells?
options: Within 2 hours
Within 24 hours
Within 8 hours
Within 3 days
questions.explain: CLSI guidance calls for separating serum or plasma from cells within 2 hours of collection unless stability data show otherwise. Cells continue to use glucose and leak potassium, which changes results.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Processing (glycolysis)
questions.q: A red top tube for glucose sits unspun for 5 hours. How is the result likely affected?
options: Falsely high glucose
No change in glucose
Falsely low glucose
Falsely high calcium
questions.explain: Blood cells consume glucose, so it falls by a measurable amount each hour in unseparated serum or plasma. A gray fluoride tube or prompt separation prevents this. Calcium is not affected by glycolysis.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Processing (centrifuge operation)
questions.q: How should tubes be loaded in a centrifuge?
options: All tubes on one side of the rotor
Any arrangement, the machine self balances
Only one tube per run
Balanced, equal tubes opposite each other
questions.explain: The centrifuge must be balanced, with tubes of similar size and volume placed directly opposite each other, using a water filled tube if needed. An unbalanced load can damage the centrifuge, break tubes and create aerosols.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Processing (centrifuge operation)
questions.q: Why are stoppers kept on tubes during centrifugation?
options: To speed the clotting process
To prevent aerosols and evaporation
To make the tubes heavier
To mix the additive with blood
questions.explain: Spinning open tubes can release infectious aerosols and allows evaporation, which concentrates the sample. Tubes stay capped, and the lid is not opened until the rotor stops completely.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Processing (centrifuge operation)
questions.q: When may the centrifuge lid be opened after a run?
options: As soon as the timer reaches zero
While the rotor is slowing, to save time
Only after the rotor has stopped completely
Midway through the run to check tubes
questions.explain: Opening the lid while the rotor is moving risks injury and aerosol release. Most centrifuges lock the lid until the rotor stops, but staff should wait for a full stop regardless.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Processing (aliquoting)
questions.q: Which practice is correct when aliquoting serum into a transfer tube?
options: Use a pipette and label the new tube
Pour serum into a clean unlabeled tube
Use a mouth pipette for accuracy
Pour the cells and serum together
questions.explain: Serum is transferred with a disposable pipette, avoiding the cell layer, and each aliquot tube is labeled with the same patient identifiers and specimen type as the original. Mouth pipetting is prohibited, and pouring risks spills and cell carryover.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Processing (labeling)
questions.q: When should blood tubes be labeled?
options: Right after collection, at the bedside
Before the draw, to save time
At the lab once all of the tubes arrive
At the end of the shift in a batch
questions.explain: Tubes are labeled right after collection at the patient's side, and the labels are compared with the patient's identification. Prelabeling or labeling away from the patient increases the risk of wrong patient errors.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Processing (labeling)
questions.q: Which information is required on a specimen label?
options: Patient name and hospital room number only
Test name and price
Two identifiers, date, time and initials
Provider phone number and diagnosis
questions.explain: A specimen label needs at least two patient identifiers, such as full name and date of birth or ID number, plus collection date and time and the collector's initials, according to facility policy. Room numbers are not identifiers.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Processing (rejection criteria)
questions.q: Which specimen will most likely be rejected by the laboratory?
options: A properly filled light blue tube
An unlabeled tube
A gold SST spun after clotting
A lavender tube mixed right away
questions.explain: Unlabeled specimens are rejected because their source cannot be confirmed. The other options describe correctly handled specimens. Other common rejection reasons are mislabeling, hemolysis for certain tests, clotting and wrong tube type.

questions.ref: NHA CPT test plan 2025, Processing (rejection criteria)
questions.q: A potassium specimen arrives visibly hemolyzed. What usually happens?
options: It is tested and reported without comment
It is diluted with saline and tested
It is spun again to remove hemolysis
